newsitem.title: INDIA: INTERVIEW-Hutchison Max to double India investment.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-Hutchison Max to double India investment.

text.p: Cellular telephone operator Hutchison Max Telecom plans to double its investment in India's growing cellular market within the next couple of years, a senior company official said on Friday.

"We have already invested around 5.0 billion rupees ($140 million) in the last one and a half years and we will invest another 5.0 billion in the next two years," Ashwani Windlass, the firm's managing director, told Reuters in an interview.
Hutchison Max, which has among the most lucrative cellular licenses for the commercial capital of Bombay, is a venture of Max India and Hong Kong's Hutchison Whampoa.
Windlass said the firm planned to invest in expanding its operations and purchasing a stake in other cellular licenses.
"In the next one year we should have two to three licenses by tying up with people who already have licenses," he said.
Global telecommunications firms including U.S. West, AT&T Corp, France Telecom and Telekom Malaysia have partnered local companies for cellular licenses in the country.
Windlass said Hutchison Max was likely to end the current fiscal year 1996/97 -- running from April through March -- with around 65,000 to 68,000 subscribers.
Analysts say there are around 100,000 cellular subscribers in Bombay. The other cellular licensee in the city is BPL Cellular -- a venture of India's BPL Group and France Telecom.
"We expect an additional 80,000 to 100,000 subscribers in the next fiscal," Windlass said.
He pegged average monthly usage time per subscriber at around 200 minutes. A subscriber paid an annual bill of 12,000 to 18,000 rupees, he said.
"In Bombay, our expectation is that until you come to half a million subscribers, the airtime should be at least 200 minutes a month on the average," Windlass said.
"If while penetrating newer brackets, we are able to maintain 200-225 minutes per user that makes a good target."

India began opening its telecommunications sector as part of its gradual conversion to a free-market economy from 1991. Cellular operators launched services in 1995, starting with the four metros of Bombay, Calcutta, New Delhi and Madras.

He said the firm's plan to launch an issue of American Depositary Receipts (ADRs) had been put on hold after an ADR issue by BPL Cellular was withdrawn last December. BPL was forced to withdraw the issue due to poor sentiment for India.
"We had a plan but we had to defer it. I don't see the issue happening in the first half of 1997," Windlass said.
He said a large number of U.S. firms were vying to attract investments for new licenses in their telecommunications sector and an Indian issue was unlikely to get a good response.
Questions about the regulatory framework which governed the industry still remained, he said.

Windlass said a recent controversy sparked by the Department of Telecommunications' (DoT) decision to sharply hike the rate of a phone call from a basic phone to a cellular unit in all states except the four metros -- would hit the industry.
"It was not something they understood from the tender conditions. Now the high license fee has become questionable."

Windlass said the move could make lenders re-evaluate their commitments to these projects. "The lenders basically look at the securitiy of the risk and the risk becomes bad the moment you see the regulatory environment changing," he said.
